case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3-11-2008 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 2919 of 2006)
full_judgment:
Md Muzammel Hossain CJ: This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 3-11-2008 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.2919 of 2006 making the Rule absolute.

2. The present respondents being the writ petitioners filed Writ Petition No.2919 of 2006 before the High Court Division stating, inter alia, that the writ petitioners having obtained Bachelor of Homeopathic degree in Medicine and Surgery (BHMS) from Bangladesh Homeopathic Medical College and Hospital under the University of Dhaka, filed applications for the posts of Lecturer of Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka pursuant to the Notification issued by the office order of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare vide Memo No. Jana Sastha-l/Homeo-4 /93/ 28 dated 25-1-1999. After completion of necessary formalities these 7 (seven) petitioners were selected as part-time teachers of the said college provisionally without pay. The order of appointment of the writ petitioners was communicated to them by the Director General of Health Directorate vide its Memo No. Sha: Adhi: / Ho:De: /97/Niyog /65/80/1(11) dated 22-2-1999 (Annexure-A series) under the signature of the Director of the Homeo and Indigenous Treatment on behalf of the Director General (DG), Health Directorate, Mohakhali, Dhaka.

3. Having obtained appointments the writ petitioners joined in their respective posts in the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka and accordingly the Principal of the College accepted their joining letters and distributed their classes. The acceptance of the joining letters of the writ petitioners and distribution of classes were communicated to them vide Memo No.HDC/46/92 dated 11-3-1999 (Annexure-B series). After joining their respective posts the writ petitioners have been performing their duties sincerely, honestly and diligently with the full satisfaction of the students and the college authority. Nobody raised any objection against the performance of the writ petitioners.

4. An Inspection Committee of the University of Dhaka consisting of Professor Dr. Chowdhury Mahmud Hasan, Dean of the Faculty of Pharmacy, the University of Dhaka, Professor Dr. Abul Hasan, Botany Department and Mr. Mohammad Ershad Ali, Inspector of Colleges (in charge), University of Dhaka after completion of inspection submitted report wherein they recommended for extension of the registration of the college for the sessions 1997-2001 to teach BHMS course subject to the fulfillment of 13 conditions of which condition Nos.2 and 5 are reproduced below. “(২) সিলেবাস অনুযায়ী প্রতিটি বিষয়ের জন্য ১(এক) হস সগযোগী অধ্যাপক, ২(দুই) জন সহকারী অধ্যাপক এবং ৩(তিন) জন প্রভাষক নিয়োগ করতে হবে।(3)-----(4)---(5) কলেজের উপযুক্ত শিক্ষা দানের স্বার্থে যে সব শিক্ষককে অবৈতনিক ভাবে নিয়োগ দেয়া হয়েছে তাদের নিয়মিত পূর্বকালীন শিক্ষক হিসাবে নিয়োগ দানের ব্যবস্থা করতে হবে।”.

5. In view of the report of the Inspection Committee of the University of Dhaka, the Syndicate of the University of Dhaka approved the said recommendations in its meeting dated 3- 6-2000 and extended the registration of the College subject to the fulfillment of the said 13 conditions.

6. The decision of the University Syndicate was communicated by the Inspector of Colleges, University of Dhaka vide Memo No.313/ K:P: dated 7-6-2000 under the signature of the Inspector of Colleges, University of Dhaka to the Principal of the Homeopathic Degree College. Similar letter was again issued after holding inspection on 30-10-2005.

7. In view of the repeated letters and reminders of the, University of Dhaka, the Academic Council and the Syndicate, the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital Authority wrote a letter to the Director General, Health Directorate, Mohakhali, Dhaka stating that as per Project Profile of the College the post of Lecturer should be created and the writ petitioners be appointed as full-time teachers/regular teachers of the said college in accordance with the direction of the University of Dhaka. The said letter was communicated to the DG Health Directorate by the Principal of the College under Memo No.HDC 46/92/2112 dated 11-12-2001.

8. In pursuance of the aforesaid direction/condition Nos. 2 and 3 of the Syndicate of the University of Dhaka as well as request of the college authority, the Director (Admin) on behalf of the DG Health Directorate, by its office Memo No. Sha Adhi: /Prosha-2/ Homio-61/99/6442 dated 13-2-2002 along with relevant documents communicated to the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to create 64 new posts in the revenue set up.

9. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by its Memo No. Jana Sastha-1/ Homeo- 8/2001/11 dated 8-1-2003 (Annexure-G) issued under the signature of the Senior Assistant Secretary along with relevant documents requested the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment to create 64 posts in fulfillment of the condition Nos.2 and 5 imposed by the Syndicate of the University of Dhaka in its meeting dated 3-6-2000.

10. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by another letter issued under Memo No. Jana Sastha-1/Homeo-8/2001/203 dated 21-5- 2003 (Annexure-H) again requested the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment to grant approval to the creation of 64 new posts for regularization of the services of eight honorary teachers of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka in compliance with aforesaid direction.

11. In the meantime all on a sudden the DG, Health Directorate, most abruptly, malafide and arbitrarily released the writ petitioners-respondents from their services. They made a representation to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare who by its Memo No. Jana Sastha-1/Homeo-4/93/116/1(4) dated 24-3-2003 (Annexure-I) passed under the signature of the Senior Assistant Secretary, stayed the said decision releasing the writ petitioners-respondents from the service of the college and directed them to join in their respective posts and inform the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. Accordingly the said order of release of the writ petitioners-respondents from service was stayed and the writ petitioners continued to serve as teachers of the college.

12. Pursuant to the aforesaid memo dated 24- 3-2003 the Principal of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka allowed the writ petitioners to continue their service in the college and directed them to take their respective classes. The Principal of the college communicated the said letter to the DG Health and others vide his Office Memo HDC 83/ 2002/791/15 (18) dated 5-5-2003 (Annexure-1).

13. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare again by its Memo No. Jana Sastha-/Momeo-8/2001/320 dated 4-8-2003 (Annexure- K) under the signature of the Senior Assistant Secretary requested the Ministry of Establishment for granting approval of 64 posts to regularize on full-time basis the services of eight honorary teachers without pay as per conditions Nos.2 and 5 contained in the direction dated 3-6-2000 of the Syndicate of the University of Dhaka.

14. In pursuance of the aforesaid letters of the Dhaka University Authority, the Principal of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka, the Health Directorate and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the Ministry of Establishment by its Office Memo No. Sha:M: /Team-5(2) 79/95-97 dated 11-5-2004 (Annexure-L) created 47 new posts for the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka and communicated the same under the signature of the Senior Assistant Secretary to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

15. Thereafter the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare forwarded the said letter to the Ministry of Finance for necessary approval of the newly created 47 posts as earlier sanctioned by the Ministry of Establishment. The Ministry of Finance provisionally approved 24 posts by its office Memo No. AM / Abi: / Ba: Ni: -5 / Sastha- 20/95/337 dated 12-7-2004 (Annexure-M) issued under the signature of the Senior Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of Finance. In the said letter it approved 10 posts of Assistant Professor and 14 posts of Lecturer to be appointed or regularized for the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka.

16. The Ministry of Finance formally approved the said 24 posts stating the conditions / basis of such appointment and pay scale of the incumbent. The said approval was communicated under Memo No. AM/Abi (Basta-4)/Be: Ske (Sastha-7) 2002 (Angsha)/102 dated 2-10-2004 (Annexure-N).

17. After such approval, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare vide Memo No. Jana Sastha-1/ Homeo-8 / 2001 (Angsha) / 655/3(12) dated 23-12-2004 (Annexure-O) issued a letter to the Chief Accounts Officer of the said Ministry stating that 24 posts have been created in the revenue set up and all expenditures of the created posts for the Homeopathic Decree College would be borne by the College from its 2004-2005 revenue budget.

18. In the meantime the Authority of the University of Dhaka in order to extend the registration of the college issued a letter under Memo No.8-9 / Ka. Pa. dated 3-1-2005 (Annexure-P) to the Principal-cum-Superintendent of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka making query as to whether the condition Nos.2 and 5 and some other conditions as stated in the earlier letter had been fulfilled or not.

19. The Chairman of the Governing Body of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka and Professor of the Department of Pharmaceutical Chemistry, Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Dhaka by its letter dated 3-1-2005 (Annexure-Q) had requested the DG, Health Directorate to regularize the appointments of the honorary teachers who were appointed on 22-2-1999 as per recommendation of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and approved by the Ministry of Finance as per terms and condition Nos.2 and 5 of their earlier decision and to appoint them as Assistant Professors against the posts created pursuant to Memo dated 23-12-2004 of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.

20. The writ petitioners also filed application to the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare through the Principal of the college stating that newly created posts had been created in pursuance of the repeated directions of the Authority of the University of Dhaka as contained in Condition Nos.2 and 5 of the report of Inspection Committee. They also stated that as per the decision of the Authority of the University of Dhaka, the DG, Health Directorate wrote to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to take necessary steps for creation of 64 posts of teachers. Thereafter the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare wrote to the Ministry of Establishment for approval of 64 posts for regularization of the services of 8 honorary teachers on full-time basis. The Ministry of Finance by Memo dated 12-7- 2004 gave its necessary approval and thereafter by Memo dated 2-10-2004 the Pay Scales of the incumbents were approved but their services have not been regularized as Assistant Professor of the said college inasmuch as they have acquired vested right to be appointed / regularized as Assistant Professors of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka.

21. The Principal of the College by Memo dated 19-1-2005 forwarded to the DG, Health Directorate the applications of the honorary teachers of the college against newly created 24 posts of teachers for appointment on full-time basis. In pursuance of the said letter of the Principal, the Director General, Directorate of Health and Family Welfare by Memo dated 16-3-2005 requested the Secretary, Ministry of Health to complete the appointment procedures in respect of 24 posts on urgent basis.

22. In view of the letters dated 16-3-2005 and 19-4-2005 issued by the DG Health Directorate, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by its office memo No. Jana Sastha-1/Homeo-1/2005/ 253 dated 7-6-2005 requested him to supply the following information:

(1) whether any procedure was followed or not at the time of appointing the writ petitioners as teachers without pay and if yes, then, what was that,

(2) what is the basis for rendering service without pay for such a long time by the honorary teachers.

(3) under what provisions of law the proposal for the appointment of the honorary teachers in the newly created posts be forwarded to the Hon'ble President of the Republic?

23.	The DG, Health Directorate replied to the said queries specifically by its office Memo No.Sha: Adhi: / Ho: De: Chi: Sha: Ho: Di: Ka: / Janabal-Rajaswa / 2005/8300 dated 14-6-2005.

24.	The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare again made similar issues on 3-8-2005 and the DG, Health Directorate replied to the said queries.

25. Thereafter the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare by Memo letter dated 22-9-2005 directed the DG, Health Directorate to submit a seniority list of the teachers who have been working in the college and in response to the said letter the DG, Health Directorate submitted a seniority list of the teachers of the college.

26. When all these steps for compliance with direction of the authority of the University of Dhaka to regularize the services of the writ petitioners in the Homeopathic Degree College and thereafter creation of new posts and grant of sanction of the Ministry of Establishment and approval of the pay scale by the Ministry of Finance were going on then all on a sudden the DG, Health Directorate decided to absorb MBBS Doctors from different Medical Colleges, Hospitals and Health Directorate to the aforesaid created posts which is totally contrary to the object of creation of the said posts. In the meantime the writ respondents have appointed 8 MBBS Doctors as Lecturers in the said college.

27. In view of such absorption, the writ petitioners genuinely apprehend that their services would not be regularized inasmuch as in order to get extension of registration of the college the Authority of the University of Dhaka imposed conditions, inter alia, to appoint one Associate Professor, two Assistant Professors and three Lecturers for each subject and to regularize the services of the writ petitioners who have been serving in the college as teachers without pay for more than 7(seven) years. The aforesaid correspondences clearly show that the posts have been created for the purpose of regularization of service of the writ petitioners as Assistant Professors of the college and in view of the aforesaid correspondences, creation of posts and grant of sanction by the Ministry of Establishment and approval of the Ministry of Finance the writ petitioners legitimately expect that their services would be regularized since they have been serving in the college for the last 7(seven) years continuously without pay. The action of the writ respondents have taken away the legal right of the writ petitioners to be regularized as Assistant Professors of the said college.

28. In view of the letters issued by the Authority of the University of Dhaka to regularize the services of the writ petitioners in the college, the writ respondents forging up the terms and conditions imposed at the time of appointment impliedly made the temporary service of the writ petitioners permanent and have been receiving their service for the last seven years.

29. A Division Bench of the High Court Division after hearing both parties by the impugned judgment and order dated 3-11-2008 made the Rule absolute directing the Government to regularize the services of the writ petitioners with regular appointment as Lecturers/Assistant Professors in the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka against the vacant posts as created vide memo dated 23-12-2004 within 2(two) months from the date of the receipt of the judgment. It was also mentioned in the judgment that the writ petitioners would get their salaries and benefits from the date of the regular appointment in the newly created posts of Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka.

30. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 3-11-2008 passed by the High Court Division, the appellants preferred the instant Civil Appeal with leave of this Court.

31. Leave was granted to consider the following submission of the petitioners:

"I. The writ petitioners i.e. respondent Nos.1 to 7 were appointed as part time teachers on temporary basis without any pay and allowances and they joined there accepting the terms and conditions of temporary and contractual service and, as such, the writ petitioners by the temporary appointment did not get any legal right to regularize them in newly created revenue posts and on the other hand, the respondent Nos. l to 7 are neither holders of constitutional post nor employees of any statutory post nor performing any duty of public character nor Government servants and, as such, the writ petition in view of above facts and circumstances is not maintainable in its present form and manner and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside.

II. Since the writ petitioners i.e. respondent Nos. 1 to 7 were appointed as teachers on temporary and contractual basis, they neither got any legal right nor vested right to regularize themselves in the newly created revenue posts as a matter of right and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside.

III. The High Court Division committed wrong and illegality in making the Rule absolute on the basis of recommendation of an Inspection team of Dhaka University though the aforesaid recommendation is neither law nor rule which may confer right upon the writ petitioners to regularize them in the newly created revenue posts and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set- aside."

32. Mr MK Rahman, the learned Additional Attorney General appearing for the appellants submits that the writ petitioners-respondent Nos. 1 to 7 were appointed as part-time teachers on temporary basis without any pay and allowance and they joined there accepting the terms and conditions of temporary and contractual service and, as such, the writ petitioners being employed on temporary basis could not acquire any legal right to be regularized in the newly created revenue posts and in view of the above facts and circumstances the writ petition not being maintainable in law, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division making the Rule absolute is liable to be set-aside. He then submits that the respondent Nos.1 to 7 having been employed as temporary teachers on contractual basis without any pay and allowance they neither acquired any legal right nor vested right to be regularized in the newly created revenue posts as a matter of right and, as such, the appeal is liable to be allowed. The learned Additional Attorney General finally submits that the recommendation of an Inspection Team of the University of Dhaka directing the college authority to regularize the services of the respondents appointing them as permanent teachers of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka on the basis of decisions of the syndicate as well as the Academic Council of the University of Dhaka is neither a law nor Rule which may confer right upon the respondent Nos.1 to 7 to be regularized in the newly created revenue posts and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside.

33. Mr SM Rezaul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent Nos. 1 to 7 submits that the respondent Nos.1 to 7 having obtained Bachelor of Homeopathic Medicine and Surgery (BHMS) degree under the University of Dhaka were appointed Lecturers in the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka without pay and allowance vide Memo dated 22-2-1999 of the Directorate of Health, Government of Bangladesh in pursuance of the notification issued by the Ministry of Health vide office Memo dated 1-1-1999 and the respondents joined their service in the respective posts vide Memo dated 11-3-1999 of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka and since then they have been rendering their services to the satisfaction of the Government as well as the students of the college for the last 12 years with sincerity, honesty and diligence and, as such, they are entitled to be regularized and appointed in the newly created post of teachers of the College under the revenue set up. He further submits that in view of the respondents having rendered long service as teachers without pay in the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka for more than 7(seven) years at the time of filing of the writ petition and that as per decisions and correspondences made by the Authority of the University of Dhaka, the Authority of Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka and the Directorate of Health, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare recommended for the creation of 64 posts to the Ministry of Establishment who gave sanction to 47 posts by memo dated 11-5- 2004 (Annexure-L) but finally the Ministry of Finance by memo dated 12-7-2004 (Annexure-M) approved 24 posts under revenue set up, the respondents have gained legitimate expectation to be appointed as Assistant Professors of the College as those posts have been created with the object to regularize their services in the College and the appellants' initiative to absorb MBBS degree holders to the said posts are not tenable in law and is liable to be declared to have been made without lawful authority and, as such, the appellants are liable to be directed to regularize the services of the respondents on full time basis as Assistant Professors of their respective Department of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka. He finally submits that the action taken by the appellants in transferring the MBBS degree holders (Annexure- X series) against the sanctioned posts which have been created to regularize on full-time basis the services of the honorary teachers of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka is totally unlawful and, as such, the appellants are liable to be directed to regularize the services of the writ petitioners- respondents as Assistant Professors of the said College as per letter issued by the Principal of the College vide Memo dated 19-1-2005.

34. We have heard the learned Counsels for both the parties, perused the leave granting order, impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, Concise Statements submitted on behalf of both the parties and also other materials available on record. It appears that the respondents were appointed as Lecturer in the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka without pay and allowance on temporary basis vide Memo dated 22-2-1999 issued by the Directorate of Health, Government of Bangladesh and the respondents joined their service in the respective posts and accordingly the Principal of the said College accepted their joining letters and distributed their classes. Since the date of joining, the appellants have been rendering their services without any pay and allowance till date with all sincerity, honesty and diligence to the full satisfaction of the students and the College authority. A three-member inspection team of the University of Dhaka consisting of the Dean of the Faculty of Pharmacy, the Professor of Botany Department and the Inspector of Colleges (in charge), Dhaka University after holding inspection submitted report with a direction to regularize the services of the respondent Nos. 1 to 7 as Assistant Professors of the College and to appoint according to the syllabus for each subject one Associate Professor, two Assistant Professors and three Lecturers. The relevant portion of the report reads as under:

“(১)----------

(২) সিলেবাস অনুযায়ী প্রতিটি বিষয়ের জন্য ১(এক) জন সহযোগী অধ্যাপক, ২(দুই) জন সহকারী অধ্যাপক এবং ৩(তিন) জন প্রভাষক নিয়োগ করতে হবে।

(৩)------------

(৪)----------

(৫) কলেজের উপযুক্ত শিক্ষা দানের স্বার্থে যে সব শিক্ষককে অবৈতনিক ভাবে নিয়োগ দেয়া হয়েছে তাদের নিয়মিত পুর্ণকালীন শিক্ষক হিসাবে নিয়োগ দানের ব্যবস্থা করতে হবে।”

35. But to the utter misfortune of the respondent Nos.1 to 7 they have not been regularized and appointed in the newly created posts meant for them. It also appears that in view of the repeated correspondences and reminders of the University of Dhaka, the Authority of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka wrote to the Director General, Health Directorate vide Memo dated 11- 12-2001 (Annexure-E) stating that as per project proforma of the College posts of teachers should be created and the appointments of the respondents as full-time teachers/regular teachers be made as per direction of the Authority of the University of Dhaka. In view of the direction of the Authority of the University of Dhaka as well as the prayer of the College Authority, the Director (Admin) on behalf of the Director General of Health Directorate by office Memo dated 13 - 2- 2002 (Annexure-F) sent necessary documents and particulars to the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare to create 64 more posts of teachers in the College as per condition Nos. 2 and 5 of the resolution of the meeting of the Syndicate of the University of Dhaka for appointment of teachers in the College. Thereafter the Ministry of Health vide Memo dated 8-1-2003 (Annexure-G) wrote to the Ministry of Establishment for creation of 64 posts as per terms and condition Nos. 2 and 5 of the resolution of the meeting dated 3-6-2000 of the Syndicate of the University of Dhaka. Again the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare vide Memo dated 4-8-2003 (Annexure-K) sent reminder to the Secretary, Ministry of Establishment to grant approval of 64 new posts to fulfill the aforesaid terms and conditions Nos. 2 and 5 for regularization on full-time basis of the services of eight honorary teachers of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka.

36. In the instant case the respondents having obtained BHMS Degree from the University of Dhaka were appointed lecturers in the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka without pay and allowance vide Memo dated 22-2-1999 of the Directorate of Health, Government of Bangladesh pursuant to the Notification issued by the Ministry of Health vide office Memo dated 1-1-1999 and subsequently they joined in their service in the respective posts vide Memo dated 11-3-1999. It appears that the respondents have been rendering their service as teachers of the Government Homeopathic Degree College for the last 12 years with sincerity, honesty and diligence to the full satisfaction of the students and the authority of the college. From the facts of this case it appears that the College Authority, the Director General of Health and the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare waiving the terms and conditions of the temporary, honorary and part-time service of the respondents recommended for regularization of their service by creation of 24 permanent posts under the revenue set up. By the conduct of the Director General of Health, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the Ministry of Establishment and the Ministry of Finance and also by the conduct of the College Authority the respondents were induced to continue their service with the Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital sincerely, honestly and diligently to the satisfaction of the students and the authority of the College. Relying on the recommendation, activities and conduct of the appellants, the respondents were induced to render their services voluntarily and they have rendered long 12 years’ service from the date of their joining of service in the Homeopathic Degree College and thereby the respondents have acted to their detriment by not leaving the job and seeking new employment elsewhere rather a legitimate expectation arose in the mind of the respondents that their service would be regularized in the newly created 24 posts with their seniority in their respective posts as Assistant Professors in the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka as per seniority maintained by the College Authority who in their report stated that the respondents teachers have been discharging their duties as teachers of the College sincerely, honestly and diligently to the satisfaction of all concerned.

37. The respondents rendered their service uninterruptedly from the date of joining the College and without looking for any other service under different employers and thereby the respondents acted to their detriment.

38. The admitted facts described above compel us to hold that the conduct of the appellant had an effect of a solemn promise and created legitimate expectation to the minds of the respondents that they would be appointed as permanent teacher of the college. This is why the appellants should be estopped from retreating from their promise by invoking the doctrine of promissory estoppel as well as the respondents should be given relief by applying the doctrine of legitimate expectation.

<u>39. The doctrine of promissory estoppel is an equitable conception. By this doctrine if a person makes to another a clear and unambiguous representation of fact intending that the other would act on it and if the representation transpires to be untrue, and the other does act upon it to his detriment, the representor is prevented or estopped from denying its truth.</u>

40. The doctrine of promissory estoppel was invoked by this Division in the case of Collector of Customs, Custom House, Chittagong and others vs A. Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167. In this case to avoid scarcity of sugar in the country the Government decided to import sugar under Wage Earners Scheme and waived certain formalities. The Government issued notification reducing the existing customs duty and sales tax on the importation of sugar on fulfillment of certain conditions. The respondent availed this opportunity for importing sugar at the concession- al rate of duty and sales tax fulfilling the conditions but before the arrival of the cargo and submission of the bill of entry the concessional rate was withdrawn by the Government. The Collector of Customs took the view that the respondent was not entitled to concessional rate of customs duty and taxes because the bill of entry was delivered to the customs authority after the withdrawal of the concessional rate. This Division, among other cases, discussed the case of Gujarat State Financial Corporation vs M/s. Lotus Hotels Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1983 SC 848 wherein it was held that the respondent acting upon the solemn promise made by the appellant incurred huge expenditure and if the appellant is not held to its promise, the respondent would be put in a very disadvantageous position and therefore the principle of promissory estoppel can also be invoked in this case. Applying the same principle this Division then held that the importer having acted upon the assurance given, the Government cannot retrace its steps and ask for duty at the rate mentioned in the subsequent notification. This is clearly a case of well settled principle of promissory estoppel. This Division in the case of Secretary, Ministry of Industries, Nationalised Industries Division vs Saleh Ahmed &Another and Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs Saleh Ahmed &others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 91 referring to the decision of the Central London Property Trust Ltd vs High Trees House Ltd. (1947) 1 KB 130 this Division held that the Government's decision on agreement to release the Mill in question cannot be changed with a belated plea that the decision had been revised by the Government although no such case was made out. Applying the principle of promissory estoppel it can be said that the appellant-Government cannot be allowed-to act inconsistently and the decision to release the Mill remains binding on them.

41. However, in the case of Grihayan Limited vs Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 47 DLR (AD) 12 this Division held that the, doctrine of promissory estoppel is not applicable in the case because neither in the writ petition nor in the leave petition this point was ever mooted. Neither in the writ petition nor in the leave petition the appellant had taken any ground questioning the authority of the Government to pass the impugned orders on the basis of lack of jurisdiction or the principle of promissory estoppel 42. The position of law is well settled that the Government may be estopped from refusing any representation made by it on the basis of which any person has acted to his detriment and that there is no estoppel against statute or there is no application of estoppel to prevent the performance of any constitutional or statutory duty.

43. The, Supreme Court of India having considered various decisions in the case of UP Power Corporation Ltd vs Sant Steels &Alloys (P) Ltd, AIR 2008 se 693 observed as under:

"17. In this background, in view of various decisions noticed above, it will appear that the Court's approach in the matter of invoking the principle of promissory estoppel depends on the facts of each case. But the general principle that emerges is that once a representation has been made .by one party and the other party acts on that representation and makes investment and thereafter the other party resiles, such act cannot stated to be fair and reasonable. When the State Government makes a representation, and invites the entre, primeurs by showing various benefits for encouraging making investment by way of industrial development of the backward areas or the hill areas, and thereafter the entrepreneurs on the representations so made bonafidely make investment and thereafter if the State Government resile from such benefits, then it certainly is an act of unfairness and arbitrariness. Consideration of public interest and the fact that there cannot be any estoppel against a Statute are exceptions."

44. In the case of Kasinka Trading vs Union of India and another (1995) 1 SCC 274 at page 283 paragraph 12 the Supreme Court of India expounded the doctrine as under:

"The doctrine of promissory estoppel is applicable against the Government also particularly where it is necessary to prevent fraud or manifest injustice. The doctrine, however, cannot be pressed into aid to compel the Government or the public authority to carry out a representation or promise which is contrary to law or which was outside the authority or power of the officer of the Government or of the public authority to make. There is preponderance of judicial opinion that to invoke the doctrine of promissory estoppel clear, sound and positive foundation must be laid in the petition itself by the party invoking the doctrine and that bald expressions, without any supporting material, to the effect that the doctrine is attracted because the party invoking the doctrine has altered its position relying on the assurance of the Government, would not be sufficient to press into aid the doctrine. In our opinion, the doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked in the abstract and the courts are bound to consider all aspects including the results sought to be achieved and the' public good at large, because while considering the applicability of the doctrine, the courts have to do equity and the fundamental principles of equity must forever be present to the mind of the court, while considering the applicability of the doctrine. The doctrine must yield when the equity so demands if it can be shown having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case that it would be inequitable to hold the Government or the public authority to its promise, assurance or representation."

45. In the case of Amrit Banaspati Co. Ltd. vs State of Punjab, AIR 1992 SC 1075 the Supreme Court of India observed that promissory estoppel being extension of principle of equity, the basic purpose of which is to promote justice founded on fairness and relieve a promisee of any injustice perpetrated due to promisor's going back on its promise, is incapable of being enforced in a court of law if the promise which furnishes the cause of action or the agreement, express or implied giving rise to binding contract is statutorily prohibited or is against public policy.

<u>46. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the case of Chairman, Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha vs A. Rouf Chowdhury reported in 61 DLR (AD) 28 held that the argument of promissory estoppel cannot be invoked when a permission was given to construct  the building over 60 feet in violation or contravention of any law i.e. the Civil Aviation Rules,1984 and that the sanction given on 18-2- 1993 for construction of a 22-storey building is void being contrary to the permissible limit provided in the said Rules and to the extent such permission contrary to the statutory provision is void and therefore is not permission in the eye of law and could not operate as promissory estoppel. In this case this Court has quoted with approval the decision of the case of Dr Ashok Kumar Maheshwari vs State of UP reported in AIR 1998 SC 966 wherein it has been observed that promissory estoppel cannot be invoked for enforcement of a promise or declaration which is contrary to law or outside the authority or power of the Government or person making that promise. The Supreme Court of India in Union Territory, Chandigarh Admn vs Managing Society Goswami, DGSCE reported in AIR 1996 SC 1759 held that a contract under the mandatory provisions of law can only be read and enforced in terms of the law and in no other way. The question of equitable estoppel does not arise in this case because there can be no estoppel, against statute. "</u>

47. From the above discussions it can be safely construed that by the doctrine of promissory estoppel the appellants would be estopped from denying the claims of the respondent Nos. 1 to 7 in regularizing their service in the newly created 24 posts by the appellant-Government with the purpose of regularizing the services of the respondents in their respective posts.

48. The Supreme Court of India in the case of M/S Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co, Ltd. vs State of Uttar Pradesh AIR 1979 (SC) 621 at page 644:

"But it is necessary to point out that since the doctrine of promissory estoppel is an equitable doctrine, it must yield when the equity so requires. If it can be shown by the Government that having regard to the facts as they have subsequently transpired, it would be inequitable to hold the Government to the promise made by it, the Court would not raise an equity in favour of the promisee and enforce the promise against the Government. The doctrine of promissory estoppel would be displaced in such a case because, on the facts, equity would not require that the Government should be held bound by the promise made by it. When the Government is able to show that in view of the facts which have transpired since the making of the promise, public interest would be prejudiced if the Government, were required to carry out the promise, the Court would have to balance the public Interest in the Government carrying out a promise made to a citizen which 'has induced the citizen to act upon it and alter his position and the public interest likely to suffer if the promise were required to be carried out by the Government and determine which way' the equity lies."

49. In the case of State of Rajasthan vs Mahaveer Oil Industries (1999) 4 SCC 357 at page 365 paragraph 14 Supreme Court of India observed thus:

"Public interest requires that the State be held bound by the promise held out by it in such a situation. But this does not preclude the State from withdrawing the benefit prospectively even during the period of the Scheme, if public interest so requires. Even in a case where a party has acted on the promise, if there is any supervening public interest which requires that the benefit be withdrawn or the Scheme be modified, that supervening public interest would prevail over any promissory estoppel."

50. Similarly, the Supreme Court of India in the case of Sales Tax Officer vs Shree Durga Oil Mills (1998) 1 SCC 572 held that any IPR (Industrial Policy Resolution) can be changed if- there is an overriding public interest involved.

<u>51. In the instant case the appellants have failed to show any overriding public interest that may be served by not appointing the honorary teachers to the permanent post of the college. As such, there is no bar for the application of doctrine of promissory estoppel against the appellants.</u>

<u>52. From the recommendation, conduct and activities of the College Authority, the Director General of Health, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, the Ministry of Establishment and the Ministry of Finance, we have no hesitations in holding that by the conduct of the appellants legitimate expectation arose in the mind of the respondent Nos. 1 to 7 to be absorbed / regularized on full-time basis as Assistant Professors of the Government Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur, Dhaka and, as such, the appellants should be estopped from denying the regularization of the service of the respondents.</u>

<u>53. The protection of legitimate expectation is at the root of the constitutional principle of the rule of law, which requires regularity, predictability and certainty in government's dealings with the public. In the case of Council of Civil Service I Unions vs Minister for the Civil Service (1984) 3 All ER 935 House of Lords observed that for a legitimate expectation to arise, the decision of the administrative authority must affect such person either- (a) by altering rights or obligations of that person which are enforceable by or against him in private law or (b) by depriving him of some benefit or advantage which he has in the past been permitted by the decision maker to enjoy and which he can legitimately expect to be permitted to continue to do until some rational ground for withdrawing it has been communicated to him and he has been given an opportunity to comment thereon or he has received assurance from the decision-maker that they will not be withdrawn without first giving him an opportunity of advancing reasons for contending that they should not be withdrawn.</u>

54. In the case of Sethi Auto Service Station vs Delhi Development Authority 2009 (1) SCC 180 DK Jain, J observed thus:

"32 	A case for applicability of the doctrine of legitimate expectation, now accepted in the subjective sense as part of our legal jurisprudence, arises when an administrative body by reason of a representation or by past practice or conduct aroused an expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfill unless some overriding public interest comes in the way. However, a person who bases his claim on the doctrine of legitimate expectation, in the first instance, has to satisfy that he has relied on the said representation and the denial of that expectation has worked to his detriment. The Court could interfere only if the decision taken by the authority was found to be arbitrary, unreasonable or in gross abuse of power or in violation of principles of natural justice and not taken in public interest. But a claim based on mere legitimate expectation without anything more cannot ipso facto give a right to invoke these principles."

55. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the case of SSA Bangladesh Limited vs Engineer Mahmud-ul-Islam and others reported in 24 BLD (AD) 92 = 9 BLC (AD) 84 held as under:

<u>60. The principle of legitimate expectation as enunciated in Schmidt vs Secretary of State of Home Affairs reported in (1969) 1 Ch.140 imposed upon the Government or the concerned Authorities a duty to act fairly and reasonably in dealing with the rights and for interest of the people and in case of any breach thereof the Court should act upon in striking down any order in exercise of judicial review of executive action and in case of any unreasonableness or inertness or ever latches in its part for which some or part of which benefit is lost causing prejudice to the people at large, the Court may direct the concerned to exercise its functions fairly, reasonably and in accordance with law and established principles.</u>

61. Thus the legitimacy of an action expectation can be inferred only if it is founded on the sanction of law or customs or established practice or procedure in regular or natural sequence, otherwise, it would betray the exception of the public and exercising its function fairly, reasonably and in accordance with law and principles."

56. In the case of the Chairman, Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation vs Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury reported in 22 BLD (AD) 199 at page 220, paragraph 50 this Division having quoted with approval some of the passages in Administrative law (Eighth Edition) by David Foulkes observed as under:

"doctrine of legitimate expectation comes to arise in the background of the principle that a public authority to bound. by its undertaking as to procedure it will follow provide they do not conflict with its duty (1983) 2 AC 629; if the public policy was to be changed the applicant should be given full and serious consideration whether there is some overriding public interest justifying the new departure (1984) 1 WLR 1337; a public authority has a duty to act with fairness and consistency in its dealing with the public and that if it makes inconsistent decisions unfairly or unjustly it misuse its power; existence of a regular practice which could reasonably be accepted to continue (1985) AC 374."

57. In the case of Syed SM Hasan vs Bangladesh reported in 60 DLR (AD) 76 at page 81 paragraph 31 this Court observed-

"The concept reasonable expectation has imposed a duty on the public authority to act fairly by taking into consideration all relevant factors relating to the expectation as the denial of it would amount to denial of the right guaranteed or secured and would lead to arbitrary, unfair or discriminatory treatment."

58. The Supreme Court of India while explaining the nature and scope of the doctrine of legitimate expectation in the case of Food Corporation of India vs M/s Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries (1993) 1 SCC 71 at page 76, paragraph 8 observed as under:

"The mere reasonable or legitimate expectation of a citizen, in such a situation, may not by itself be a distinct enforceable right, but failure to consider and' give due weight to it may render the decision arbitrary, and this is how the requirement of due consideration of a legitimate expectation forms part of the principle of non-arbitrariness, a necessary concomitant of the rule of law. Every legitimate expectation is a relevant factor requiring due consideration in a fair decision-making process. Whether the expectation of the claimant is reasonable or legitimate in the context is a question of fact in each case. Whenever the question arises, it is to be determined not according to the claimant's perception but in larger public interest wherein other more important considerations may outweigh what would otherwise have been the legitimate expectation of the claimant. A bona fide decision of the public authority reached in this manner would satisfy the requirement of non-arbitrariness and withstand judicial scrutiny. The doctrine of legitimate expectation gets assimilated in the rule of law and operates in our legal system in this manner and to this extent."

59. In the case of Punjab Communications Ltd. vs Union of India (1999) 4 sce727 the Supreme Court of India held that a change in policy can defeat a substantive legitimate expectation if it can be justified on "Wednesbury" reasonableness. The decision maker has the choice in the balancing of the pros and cons relevant to the change in policy. Therefore, the choice of the policy is for the decision maker and not for the Court. The legitimate substantive expectation merely permits the Court to find out if the change in pol- icy which is the cause for defeating the legitimate expectation is irrational or perverse or one which no reasonable person could have made.

60. In view of the decisions discussed above we are of the opinion that the doctrine of legitimate expectation may arise where the decision of administrative authority affects a person either by altering rights or obligations of that person which are enforceable by or against him in private law or by depriving him of some benefit which he has in the past been permitted by the decision maker to enjoy and which he can legitimately expect to be permitted to continue to do until some rational ground for withdrawing it has been communicated to him and he has been given an opportunity to comment thereon. Even legitimate expectation is a relevant factor requiring due consideration in a fair decision-making process. Whether the expectation of the claimant is reasonable or legitimate in the context is a question of fact in each case. The legitimate expectation has to be determined not according to the claimant's perception but in larger public interest wherein other more important considerations may outweigh what would otherwise have been the legitimate .expectation of the claimant. A change in policy can defeat a substantive expectation if it can be justified on "Wednesbury" reasonableness. The choice of the policy is for the decision-maker not for the Court. The legitimate substantive expectation merely permits the Court to find out if the change in policy which is the cause for defeating the legitimate expectation is irrational or perverse or one, which no reasonable person could have made. The court would interfere only if the decision taken by the authority was found to be arbitrary, unreasonable or in gross abuse of power or in violation of principles of natural justice and not taken in public interest. The principle of legitimate expectation has no role to play where the State takes action under a public policy or in the public interest and the action taken does not amount to an abuse of power. If it is not unreasonable and arbitrary, the Court must not usurp the discretion of the public authority.

61. It appears that the appellant-Government transferred MBBS Doctors to the newly. created posts of BHMS degree holders in the Homeopathic Degree College and Hospital, Mirpur and thereby locked the posts of the respondent Nos. 1 to 7 which were exclusively created for regularization of the services of the 8(eight) honorary teachers including the respondent Nos. 1 to 7 who were appointed without pay and allowance. The learned Judges of the High Court Division could not find any explanation on behalf of the appellants as to why the recommendations regarding regularization of the service of the respondent Nos. 1 to 7 as Lecturers/Assistant Professors of the Government Homeopathic Degree College could not be implemented and the learned Judges of the High Court Division rightly found that the appellant-Government failed to show why the respondents MBBS degree holders should be transferred to the Homeopathic Degree College depriving the Homeopathic Degree holders who are entitled to be appointed on full-time basis in the newly created posts of Government Homeopathic Degree College, Mirpur. The learned Judges of the High Court Division 'also rightly observed that the learned Deputy Attorney General on behalf of some of the appellants also kept mum and did not seriously oppose the contention of the respondent Nos. 1 to 7. These respondents having obtained BHMS degree of the University of Dhaka joined the Government Homeopathic Degree College, Mirpur on 11-3- 1999 and since then they have been rendering their services to the satisfaction of the students and the authority of College and because of their satisfactory service record and the need of the College to get the services of the respondent Nos.1 to 7 the Authority of the University of Dhaka, the Director General, Health, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare recommended to the Ministry of Establishment for creation of 64 posts and thereafter 24 new posts wen; created with the sanction of the Ministry of Establishment and finally the Ministry of Finance approved those posts under the revenue setup. From the aforesaid assurances, activities, conduct of the appellant-Government and the College Authority, legitimate expectation arose in the mind of the respondent Nos. I to 7 honorary teachers of the College that their service would be regularized which encouraged them to render 12 years-service in the Homeopathic Degree College to the satisfaction of the students and authority of the college and, as such, the appellant-Government will be estopped from denying the claims of the respondent Nos. I to 1, honorary teachers of the College who were appointed initially on temporary basis without pay and allowances and thereby they have acted to their detriment and that the Government- appellant and the College Authority shall be estopped by the principle of legitimate expectation to deny the regularization of the services of the respondent Nos.1 to 7 and, as such, there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in regularizing the services of the respondents as Assistant Professors with their salaries and benefits from the date of creation of the posts i.e. from 23-12- 2004 as per recommendation and seniority list prepared by the College- Authority which was approved by the Ministry of Health. We are also of the view that the doctrine  of: Promissory Estoppel is also applicable in the aid of the respondent Nos.1 to 7 who have been rendering their service with sincerity, honesty and diligence to the satisfaction of the students and the College Authority. By their conduct and activities the appellant-Government has induced or made a representation to the respondent-teachers to continue their service as honorary teachers of the Government Homeopathic Degree College without pay and allowances so that they may be regularized or appointed on full-time basis in the newly created posts under the revenue setup. In view of the above findings and observations, there is no merit in the appeal and, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order dated 3-11-2008 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.2919 of 2006 is hereby affirmed.
